title: What If God Wants to Do More Than You Ever Dared to Ask?
paragraphs:
What If God Wants to Do More Than You Ever Dared to Ask?
The Deeper Meaning of Ephesians 3:20 and the Scandalous Grace That Changes Everything
Most people read Ephesians 3:20 like a motivational quote.
A promise for bigger dreams.
A promise for more success.
A promise for greater opportunities.
Something to post when life is going well.
Something to repeat when hoping for a breakthrough.
But what if we have misunderstood it?
What if Paul was talking about something far deeper than prosperity, comfort, or personal achievement?
What if Ephesians 3:20 is not primarily about God giving you more of what you want—but about God doing something so impossibly beautiful in your life that it completely rewrites your story?
Because that is exactly what happened to Paul.
The man writing these words was once known as Saul.
A persecutor.
A hunter of Christians.
A man whose reputation was stained with violence against the very people who loved Jesus.
If social media had existed in the first century, many believers would have demanded his cancellation.
No second chances.
No forgiveness.
No redemption.
Yet the Gospel specializes in stories nobody believes can be redeemed.
That is why our theme has always been true:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
When Paul wrote Ephesians, he was not sitting in luxury.
He was imprisoned.
Chained.
Restricted.
Yet his heart overflowed with worship because he had discovered something that chains could never imprison—the limitless power of God working inside redeemed sinners.
The verse reads:
“Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us.” (Ephesians 3:20, KJV)
The original Greek text says:
Τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ ὑπὲρ πάντα ποιῆσαι ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ ὧν αἰτούμεθα ἢ νοοῦμεν
Transliterated:
Tō de dynamenō hyper panta poiēsai hyperekperissou hōn aitoumetha ē nooumen.
One word in particular nearly explodes off the page.
ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ (hyperekperissou).
Paul essentially stacks words upon words because ordinary language cannot contain what he is trying to express.
It means beyond measure.
Over and above.
Infinitely more.
Excessively beyond.
Super-abundantly greater.
Paul is reaching for vocabulary that barely exists because human language struggles to describe divine grace.
God is not limited by your imagination.
He is not constrained by your expectations.
He is not boxed in by your failures.
He is not intimidated by your history.
Because some of us secretly believe our story is already written.
The divorce defines us.
The addiction defines us.
The betrayal defines us.
The shame defines us.
The secret sin defines us.
The abortion.
The affair.
The prison sentence.
The relapse.
The years wasted.
The damage done.
The words we can never take back.
We quietly assume God can forgive us but never truly use us.
We imagine salvation as surviving rather than transformation.
But Ephesians 3:20 stands like a thunderclap across that lie.
God does not merely rescue people.
He recreates them.
The same God who transformed a Christian hunter into an apostle can transform your deepest failure into a testimony of grace.
That does not mean every earthly circumstance will unfold according to our plans.
Paul himself suffered greatly.
The verse is not a blank check for selfish desires.
The context matters.
The surrounding passage reveals Paul praying that believers would know “the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge” (Ephesians 3:19).
The greater miracle is not getting everything we want.
The greater miracle is becoming who God created us to be.
Many people ask God for relief.
God sometimes gives redemption.
Many ask for escape.
God offers transformation.
Many ask for a changed situation.
God begins by changing the person.
That is infinitely better.
The Hebrew Scriptures reveal this pattern repeatedly.
Joseph was sold by his brothers.
David was hunted.
Ruth was widowed.
Moses was exiled.
Rahab carried a scandalous past.
Yet God did not erase their stories.
He redeemed them.
The biblical idea of redemption carries the Hebrew concept of גָּאַל (ga'al)—to redeem, reclaim, rescue, and restore what appears lost.
God does not waste stories.
He rewrites them.
And nowhere is this seen more clearly than at the cross.
Humanity saw failure.
God revealed victory.
Humanity saw execution.
God unveiled salvation.
Humanity saw disgrace.
God displayed glory.
Isaiah prophesied centuries earlier:
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.” (Isaiah 53:5)
What looked like history's greatest scandal became history's greatest rescue mission.
The cross is proof that God can bring unimaginable beauty from unimaginable brokenness.
That is why Ephesians 3:20 should never be reduced to positive thinking.
It is a declaration about the limitless power of God displayed through Jesus Christ.
The God who raised Christ from the dead is still working.
Still healing.
Still restoring.
Still calling prodigals home.
Still rewriting stories that appear beyond repair.
Maybe that is why this verse has survived centuries.
Because deep down, every human heart longs to believe that failure is not the final chapter.
That shame does not get the last word.
That regret is not stronger than grace.
That Jesus still transforms lives.
And perhaps that longing is why you are still reading.
Maybe there is a part of your story you have hidden from everyone else.
The chapter you hope nobody discovers.
The memory that still wakes you up at night.
The mistake that still whispers accusations.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not deny your sin.
It defeats its authority.
The Gospel does not minimize your past.
It magnifies Christ's power to redeem it.
The Gospel does not say you were never broken.
It proclaims that Jesus is a greater Savior than your deepest failure.
That is the deeper meaning of Ephesians 3:20.
God is able to do far more than you can ask or imagine—not merely around you, but within you.
Not merely for you, but through you.
Not merely in your circumstances, but in your soul.
And if He can transform Saul into Paul, a cross into salvation, and a grave into resurrection, He can certainly rewrite your story too.
Be honest.
Did this hit somewhere deep?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
You never know which soul is one moment away from discovering that grace still has the final word.
And perhaps the greatest miracle God performs is not changing your circumstances overnight—but refusing to stop writing your story until it looks more like Jesus.
